utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received French translation on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The registrar has told us that this was -- this is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to continue your examination of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then like to remind Mr. Simic that, Mr. Simic, you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of the testimony that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President if I could just inform Court the redacted documents, P967 and 968, MFI have been uploaded and also with regard to the translations of P972, the cover page has been uploaded and yesterday I made a mistake when I referred to chapter 7. There is no chapter 7. It was chapter 15 and chapter 16. Both are translated and on e-court. But chapter 13 is not there, Mr. President. That is missing and it's still -- we are awaiting the translation to be uploaded. The translation is not complete yet. It will be done before the close of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So yesterday I think you said 17, I didn't hear 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 17, Mr. President. I just mentioned 17. When I mentioned chapter 1, 12, 13, 15, and it should have been 16, not 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now that's clear. Thank you. 13 still waiting for translation being uploaded. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar [sic], may I call document 995, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we're waiting, yesterday you called Madam Registrar Mr. Registrar. Now it is again Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't look up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I appreciate this is not a document issued by you. It is report on arrested members of enemy formations paramilitia and other persons handed over to MUP dated 7th August, 1995, submitted to the commander of the 72 Military Police Battalion by senior lieutenant Ante Renic I'd like to you take a look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar if we could go to page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There, Mr. Simic, it is reported that on 6 August 1995, the Sibenik 4th military police company workers handed over five members of enemy formations and 33 Serb civilians to the Sibenik PU collection centre. Now, before I ask you the relevant question with regard to this document, I'm going to show you another document so that we save time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call up -- can I have document number 1002, please. Before that, Mr. President so that I save time, can this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, no questions yet but then it equals tendering from the bar table. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P977 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I think we have another document now, Mr. Simic, that is report sent to Major Juric personally dated 7 August 1995, and it's a report on information with regard to the implementation of military police tasks pursuant to the OVP commander's order and there's a reference given there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar if we can move to the next page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if you could look at paragraph numbered five. It is reported that "37 RH were captured including five uniformed members of the enemy army and 33 civilians, among whom there are 12 women and 21 men (all elderly). All the above persons were captured around 1830 hours on 6th August by HV members and brought to the Sibenik military police base. Immediately after their details were recorded, they were escorted to the Baldekin centre in Sibenik." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Translation is now being finished. May I take it that 37 is a slip of the tongue and should be 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You mean the civilians, Mr. President? Oh, yeah, 38. It should be 38. I said 38, probably it got recorded as 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- yes. I heard 37, and it was transcribed as 37. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now my question to you is, Mr. Simic, why was civilians being captured by the HV and taken to collection centres? Yes. Mr. Simic, I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could we first try to find out what RH stands for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, is it possible for you to explain what that abbreviation is, RH, in -- mentioned in paragraph -- paragraph 5? Just after the number 38. In the B/C/S version there is some text and then "38 RH and OD," something are you able to tell Court as at the what that means?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that in the document, 38 RH, but I don't know what that acronym stands for. It's not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph, this information relates to activity of the Sibenik military police 4th Company, of which you were a senior officer. So are you able to tell Court as to why civilians were being captured according to -- it is reported here, and taken to collection centres. What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that. I can only assume that the intention was to protect them. But I don't know, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you as a member of the military police have -- did you receive any instructions as to how to deal with civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there appear to be no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P978 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document 1744, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just for the record, note my position is preserved in the future, I believe the last question and answer were vague in terms of what was meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a report on activities undertaken by the military crime police for 12th August 1995 by 0830 hours -- the report is dated 12 August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could, Mr. Registrar, move to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could look at the report relating to the Sibenik Company, in the last paragraph of that particular section, it's reported in this manner: "There are still only five persons at the reception centre for civilians, while a total of 80 of them have been driven to a new reception centre on the island of Obonjan. The number of prisoners here also keeps changing constantly, given that new arrivals are coming in all the time and persons are being released from the centre." Now, are you able to offer an explanation to the Trial Chamber as to why civilians were being treated as prisoners, which is what is reported here, and this is a report relating to your military police company.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document I've just seen now. I am not familiar with it from before. I don't know who the author of the document is, and I don't know why it has been written that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show who the author of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we move to page 4 of the English version and page 2 -- 3 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could get a clarification from Ms. Mahindaratne she is saying these are civilians at the centre, and I'm not finding that in the text. If she could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first for one second finish what we're doing. That is, to identify who is the author and then go back to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because otherwise we're moving from one page to another without getting answers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know the author of this document? Who is this person, Ante -- it says department chief as Ante Glavan, senior lieutenant. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you dealt with that person, spoken with that person, received instructions from him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from him. He is a member of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When it says department chief, what exactly was his role?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was the commander or the head of the MP department up at the MP administration. He definitely worked the MP administration and I could not have gotten in touch with him without my superior or, rather, without going through my superior, Boris Milas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, I now you were attached to the crime military police department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I allowed you to identify the person who's the author and then to deal with the matter raised by Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I just tried to read -- in fact Mr. Misetic wanted to know where I got the word civilian it is recorded here there are still only five persons at the reception centre for civilians while a total of 80 of them have been driven to a new reception centre on the island of Obonjan. The number of prisoners here also keeps changing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, Ms. Mahindaratne is reading the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It says it was a centre for civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the exceptions, assumptions, things like that, that is put the question. The second point is that apparently I have when the list was initially closed to us have one translation, and apparently there is now a second translation of it in e-court. So there must have been a new English translation uploaded into e-court of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Whenever we upload revised translations, the parties with informed Mr. President. An e-mail sent from trial support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like it know what the new translation says. That is it more of interest to me at this moment. There is an new translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless even with the new translation, Your Honour, I would ask that assumptions not be in posing the question that she reads the text as it is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I did Mr. President. I did it exactly verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at that. We can check that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And also Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look at one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also make an objection at this point even to the translation on the screen with respect to the second sentence because although it is in slashes, of prisoners. That doesn't appear in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The slashes caught my attention as well, Ms. Mahindaratne. And that there's not in the original. Could you explain -- have you given it some thought on why -- perhaps not an important word like the number of prisoners -- why that appears in slashes and what that means in relation to the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I presume, Mr. President generally the slashes come when the interpreters are not certain of a translation but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you seek any confirmation of -- because if the interpreters are not certain we should clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President but what I have the clarification I had at the OTP is that it does -- it is not incorrect the term the prisoners. Now, if native speaker says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's check that. I am aware that I'm going a bit beyond what I should do. We see that in English the words the number and then between slashes of prisoners appear. If I would start reading the original text and it should be interpreted, if someone could read it. Because my pronunciation will be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to, Your Honour. It's the last sentence in section 2. It is [interpretation]: "Here, too, the number keeps constantly changing, in view of a continued arrival of new comers and of the persons from the centre being released." [In English] So, Your Honour, my objection is the word prisoners didn't appear in the text anywhere, so I don't know it would be inserted in slashes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That remains an issue. Ms. Mahindaratne, we have now heard how it was interpreted. Could you please submit this document for verification of the translation, especially of the portion between the dashes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's being done right now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's me also add that -- apparently I'm now told that this translation was disclosed to us last night. I'm sorry. October 6th, I apologise. But the previous translation had the words -- it says even on this location the number of prisoners keeps changing -- and the "of prisoners" isn't even in slashes in the first one, so that would suggest to me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the more reason to have the translation being verified specifically of this sentence, Ms. Mahindaratne. We have now -- the line was read to us. It was translated. And I do understand that the word "prisoner" as such does not appear in this sentence. Then the other issue was civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was Mr. President from the first line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that. Mr. Misetic, what I see there, that it's mentioned, reception centre for civilians. That's how it reads. While a total of 80 of them, of them, I have difficulties to understand it to refer to five persons, because 80 out of five is not possible. Neither would I consider that "of them" would relate to reception centres. So, therefore, I am inclined to understand total of 80 of them to refer to civilians. I'm just giving you -- for the time being, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just advise the Chamber that in the prior translation, it was translated "I believe more accurately that there are still only five persons at the civilian collection centre. A total of 80 persons have been transferred to a new collection centre on the island of Obonjan." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That portion of the document, the translation should also be verified, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will check with Ms. Mahindaratne during the break as to why a new translation was requested in the first place and then we'll report back to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I can explain right now Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Ms. Mahindaratne, why not give it some thought, try to have everything verified and then inform the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But I could just inform court that it wasn't a case of a new translation being requested but this is the revised translation that is done with regard do all documents. It is initially at a draft stage and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I do believe there were good reasons to replace it. What I'm interested in and I take it my colleagues as well is the right translation is. That's what we care about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do so, Mr. President. For the time being, Mr. President, may I tender in a -- and a number be given an MFI status until the translation issue has been sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P979, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P979 keeps this status of marked for identification for the time being, until a final translation is uploaded and then we'll decide on admissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic one last question on that. Where is Obonjan Island, the Island of Obonjan situated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sibenik Archipelago among the Sibenik islands. But I'm not sure when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar may I have document sorry Exhibit P970, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While the document is brought up Mr. Simic your testimony was that you initiated the investigation into the killing incidents of Varivode, Gosici, and Zrmanja pursuant to request from the Zadar county prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I was engaged only in some of the segments of all that. I was just investigating the reasonable doubts that murders had been committed but I did not have any knowledge of that being a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, my question was who requested you to conduct the investigation. That was my question. Who instructed you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military prosecutor's office in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when did you commence the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I received the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When, as in now there is a note front of us dated 25th October. So did you start it week before? I'm just asking for the time-frame, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to remember. But if you had the complete -- the complete case file I'm sure you will be able to see that. If you have a note of that, I'm sure that you will also have the complete case file.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked to cease investigations on 25th October, had you been involved in the investigation or have you been -- had you been conducting investigations for a while, before that? And when I say "for a while," I'm talking about one or two weeks or was it a couple of days before.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say how many days. Because this was not the only case I was involved in. There were other cases. But I repeat, if you have the note then you also have the complete case file, and I'm sure you will be able to find the exact date of when the investigation began.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask for the exact date. Just approximately are you able to tell how many dies were involved in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to remember. I can't remember. I'm -- I may be wrong I may give you a wrong number, a wrong date and I don't want to do that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us approximately, was it a couple of days, approximately a week, and a week could be anything between five, or eight, or nine days. Give us just when possible an indication of the time you had spent on the investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I gave you any figure, it would just be a wild guess and I don't know if that would be of any use either to me or to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me just take you to that paragraph numbered 1 there, Mr. Simic. There an a detail there, Goran Vunic, son of Ante, born on 4 October 1973 in Sibenik, residing in Ladevci and there are details and about -- the next line there says: Together with two others as of yet unidentified men, he has shot and killed Gojko Lezajic in the courtyard of his house in Gosici. The neighbours have buried the body at the local cemetery (statements given by) ..." and there are two names. Now this is a note that you wrote. From where did you obtain that information, that Goran Vunic had committed this crime in the manner that you have described, in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the municipal prosecutor's office in Zadar. Sava Letunica and Milan Letunica provided statements in Zadar, about the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you examine those statement yourself; did you read those statements?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you reported to Captain Mrkota on the 25th, did you inform him of all these details?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you also inform him that there was a search warrant issued by the military judge in Sibenik for you to search the premises of Goran Vunic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I did, I reported to Captain Mrkota.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was there any other military police departments other than your section involved in this investigation? And I'm talking about not the Ministry of Interior but military police, crime police sections, involved in this investigation other than your section, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your section, who led the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was in charge, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now when you informed Captain Mrkota on the 25th October that you were intending to take some steps, did you make him aware that what were you going to do was to search the premises of Goran Vunic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, you were within the military police crime police until 2004. At any time after 25th October did you ever learn that Goran Vunic had been named as a witness, or an informant, or had assisted in any way in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date that you have just mentioned, I'm not sure about the date. Would you please repeat your question, because there's wrong with the date that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, what I mentioned was, you know, after this date, 25th October 1995 after you were ordered to cease investigation by your commander, did you at any time learn; or did you get any information until the time you left the military police in 2004, that Goran Vunic had been used in this investigation as an informant or a witness?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Goran Vunic's processing continued whether there was still investigation against him, I don't know. That was not my level and there was no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think that answers my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document Exhibit P203, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, I appreciate this is not a document that you ought to be familiar with necessarily. This is report sent to the minister of defence. I'd like you to look at paragraph 4 of this document, where it is reported that in the liberated area of the hinterlands of Zadar and Sibenik, the establishment of the civilian authorities is not being carried out in a satisfactory pace. More precisely: "In the liberated settlements Bribirski Mostine, Djevrske and Kistanje the situation is rather chaotic. Incidents of mass burning of houses plundering of property, alcohol consumption occur and the units lack organisation. The reason for such a situation is the insufficient engagement of the command personnel of the units." Now were you ever ordered by your commander, Captain Mrkota, to conduct any criminal investigations into crimes perpetrated in Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything that happened in Kistanje was not subject of my discussions with Captain Mrkota, nor did I receive any orders from him to undertake an investigation in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think I have just one more question, specifically in regard to the exclusion of the statement, as regards the agreement yesterday. Mr. Registrar could I have P968, please, supplementary statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this a redacted supplementary statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could go to next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I'd like to you look at paragraph 5 of the statement in front of you, which is your supplementary statement, where you say, and you are making a correction to your previous statement. You say: "In paragraph 20, it should be stated that a brigade commander, whose member has committed a serious crime, would send a proposal to the Military District Commander to discharge the perpetrator from the service." Now, my question to you is: Was there a requirement that the member of the brigade against whom a disciplinary punishment is sought should have been found guilty of the crime pursuant to a disciplinary inquiry prior to the submission of the proposal for dismissal by the brigade commander to the Military District Command?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Pursuant to Rule number 5, grave crimes committed by Croatian army soldiers, active servicemen, the proposal was sent to the military prosecutor's office, and it was the military prosecutor's office who dealt with their status. If a crime had indeed been committed, a decision was -- waited for, and if we're talking about reserve force, those people were discharged through the department for defence, i.e., their status as member of the Croatian army ceased.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what were the circumstances in which a brigade commander would submit a proposal for dismissal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it assumes a fact not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well I referred him to the paragraph which is already --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which we were going to lead live. It is not in evidence. It was to be led live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must say that that confused me a bit what was to be taken out and what was to be led live. But nevertheless stayed in. It was your agreement and you made that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, Your Honour, I assume she wasn't going to show him the statement before leading it live but it will be easier for me now to do the same on cross so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's please rephrase your question, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if you could -- could you try to explain, what happens for instance when a member of a brigade is found to have looted, for instance, was found to have stolen some private property. What would the brigade commander's duty be in such instances if such a report received -- reached him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object on vagueness grounds, Your Honour; what circumstances. We've gone now to a different area that was initially deposited to the witness which was after a conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is exactly apparently the issue we're trying to clarify. If a brigade commander would receive a report without there being a conviction yet, but receiving a report, that one of the members of his brigade was reported as having been looting, what would that brigade commander have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, in almost all cases, that is, we waited for the outcome of the criminal report, if the criminal report was accepted, a request would be sent to the military prosecutor's office if the perpetrator was an active policeman. If the person was a mobilised person a person who had been mobilised through the department for defence that person would have been discharged from the Croatian army through the same department of defence that originally mobilised him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said if the perpetrator was an active policeman, is that what you meant to say? Or did you say a member of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, an active serviceman, a active member of the armed forces. Both were members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not limited to policemen. Now, how much time did it take if someone was reported of having looted until such a criminal report was prepared and accepted? How much time would that take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depended largely on the case. It all depended on how fast material evidence was collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You yesterday told us when you were asked about a long list of goods that were seized, that you didn't know whether any further investigation took place, in relation to that, which opens the possibility that such a criminal report would never being made and would be accepted. What I wanted to know from you is whether your answer comes down to soon after this was reported, he would -- it would be proposed that he should be discharged of his duties or whether, in fact, in most of the cases, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see how nothing could have happened. The military crime report police section, when they submitted a report against an unknown perpetrator, they would also inform the brigade that such a request had been filed. They wouldn't file a request to the military prosecutor's office or ask for their discharge from the army. That was an obligation and a duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is whether in all of these cases or in most of these cases, finally a military crime report -- a crime report would be prepared. I mean, I do understand that if it would be prepared and would be accepted then perhaps action would be taken. But what I'm interested in to know is whether such crime reports in this period of time, in your area of responsibility, were prepared, were submitted, and were accepted or whether, in whatever percentage of the cases, this would not be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course such reports were sent to the prosecutor's office, and if there were elements for their acceptance, they would be accepted. And if there were no such elements then they would not be accepted. But we did not have a say in that. It was up to us to prepare report, with all the enclosers and attachments, the material evidence and everything else that was necessary, and refer the case file to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked you in relation to a rather long list of approximately close to 100 items where the goods were seized, whether any follow-up investigations took place at all, and you said you couldn't tell us, you don't know. Today you tell us that crime reports would usually be made. I would like to reconcile the answer you gave yesterday with the answers you give today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Applying to all crimes. And yesterday I spoke about the list. I don't know anything about the list. I don't know whether any of the people on that list were eventually prosecuted or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday whether when seeing such a list you could tell us whether follow-up would be given if someone was found to be in the possession of goods that most likely had been looted, and you said you couldn't tell us whether, in such cases, that any follow-up investigation would take place and you explained what the problems were to do so. Now, today are you suggesting, although in general terms, that crime reports would be prepared in all these cases. What I'd like to know is what actually happened, whether in most of these cases crime reports were prepared, were submitted, and were accepted; or whether in many of these cases they would just not be prepared and submitted? And I'm not asking this question in general terms and what should have been done, but concrete -- concretely, on what was done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring concretely to the list that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the cases as described in many documents. The many cases where people were found in possession of goods they were suspected to have looted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand your question, the military police had to report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- anybody they caught red-handed on the way of looting or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there already. You said what the military police had to do. What I want to know is what the military police actually did, in most of these cases.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In most cases, they did act pursuant to the rules and criteria that were in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, under those circumstances, there must have been a huge number of -- a very large number of crime reports on looting. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's possible is -- I ask you whether it's your recollection that there was a large number of crime reports concerning looting. Not whether that is it possible but whether you have a clear recollection that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many do you remember, approximately? In your area of responsibility, in your function, well, let's say, the first ten days after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is very difficult to talk about that. I can only speak about monthly periods because we sent our reports every month. The military crime police section sent very few reports, but in the area there were also the MUP and 71st military police, and if you added everything up together, then the number of crime reports would be rather large and especially if you take into account the MUP reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about the criminal police crime reports, the criminal police -- military police crime reports, not about the MUP. Could you tell us approximately how many you remember to have seen in the first monthly period after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we saw the report that the military crime police section of the 4th Sibenik Company submitted. That is also a list of criminal reports, and that's much as I know. I don't know anything else. If you exclude MUP and if you exclude the 71st Battalion, then that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're telling us all the crime reports are found in that document we saw yesterday, excluding MUP, excluding the 71th Battalion. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I say please proceed, I said yesterday that I would keep you to a time-limit, which was already -- you have passed that when I asked a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President if I could just have three minutes I will wrap up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three minutes. You've got three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, Mr. Simic, yesterday we saw a document which you are familiar with, rules governing the structure an operation of military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record, that was P880.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And we looked at Article 61 there where there was a requirement that the military police had to inform the senior-most officer of the unit to which the perpetrator belonged, when the military police -- had raised a criminal report in relation to an offence. It is Article 61, Mr. Misetic. Now, according to that requirement, once the military police informed the senior-most officer, let us say, an example, a brigade commander was informed that a member of his brigade had committed a crime, what could he do? What was he expected to do?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained this a moment ago and I will try to have another go. If the person involved was an active serviceman most often one waited for the outcome of the criminal report, i.e., whether it was accepted or not. In that case, the proposal was sent to the military prosecutor's office for breaches of discipline. If the individual was a reserve serviceman who had been mobilised by the department for defence then he would be dealt with through the department for defence which does not exclude the possibility for a criminal report to be filed against him, and that particular course of action would be carried out in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who would initiate that process where the -- the mobilised personnel were dealt with through the department? Who would initiate that process once the brigade commander is informed?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question or clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You just said if the individual was a reserve serviceman who been mobilised by the department for defence, then he would be dealt with through the department for defence. So who would initiate that process where he can be dealt with or disciplinary measures can be meted out through the department on how -- who had the duty to initiate that process?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only competent body was the personnel service of the -- that particular brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President that concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just, in order to avoid whatever confusion, Mr. Simic, you said you've seen the report yesterday. The report yesterday, I think, Ms. Mahindaratne has put to you, was talking about eight crimes, one report -- crime report having been prepared. Is that what you were referring to in your earlier answer when you said you have seen the statistics yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I meant that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just put to you how I do understand your testimony and, please correct me when I'm wrong. You said action would be taken against an active member of the armed force once a crime report would have been accepted. I then asked you whether if crime report would be made, whether that would not be a very large number of crime reports, because in my question I raised the issue of whether in all cases, crime reports were made. You said, Yes, that should be a large number. Then I asked you whether you had any recollection of the numbers as such, and then you said, Well, if you do not include MUP and the 71st Battalion, then you'll find the results in the report we looked at yesterday. Now, yesterday we looked at a report where it was mentioned that one crime report was submitted. I'm just explaining to you what I understand your testimony is, so in order to give you an opportunity to correct me if my understanding is wrong. Is my understanding right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that what's unclear is how the disciplinary procedure against an active serviceman is initiated. That's to say against a professional member of the army. I said that where a criminal report is filed and where it is accepted by the prosecutor's office, then the proceedings are initiated because there already exists material evidence as to his guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is not a comment on my understanding of your testimony, in terms of numbers, and that's what I focussed on. Thank you for that answer, Mr. Simic. Mr. Misetic, you will be the first one to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have on the screen 1D56-0005?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic this is the document that the Presiding Judge showed you yesterday. I think we've already gone through verification of your signature so we don't need to do that any longer --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just, as in the case of how it is dealt with, the Prosecution statements. If the Defence statement is to be put to the witness and since he has had the opportunity to now peruse, perhaps it might be appropriate to ask the witness perhaps by the Trial Chamber by Your Honours if he has any corrections to make to this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see what Mr. Misetic has asked the statement to be on the screen. Let's see how he proceed with them because I do understand that he want to tender them under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I take it that the usual attestations will be sought and if there's any problem with that I'm always willing to assist the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you were given this statement yesterday to review. Were you able to review the document yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you gave to investigators of the Gotovina Defence team in July 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In reviewing that statement, was it accurate or did you find that any corrections needed to be made?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement is accurate and there is no need for any corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today again in court as you were asked in July 2008, would your answers be the same today as they were when you gave the statement in July 2008?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to Rule 92 ter I'd ask that the exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there are four paragraphs to redacted from that statement. That is page 1, paragraph 2, page 4, paragraph 2, 3 and 4 according to your agreement yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is on the screen it is redacted already Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the redact the statement has been uploaded and therefore I take it that there are no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D840 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could please go to page 4 in the English version -- oh, actually that's -- sorry. This is redacted so let me -- let me put it to you then -- I'll do it during the course of the examination, Your Honour. I will get to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding Mr. Misetic was that we paragraph 2, 3, and 4 of page 4 were to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. In the e-mail Your Honour I said paragraph 2 would be led live. Paragraphs 3 and 4 would be redacted. It's in the e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will check the e-mail. Ms. Mahindaratne, the e-mail reads: "... will the Gotovina Defence will lead live paragraph 2, page 2, will lead live paragraph 2, page 4, will remove paragraph 3, page 4, will remove paragraph 4, page 4." That's what the e-mail says. And that's what was put on the record yesterday as the agreement reached between the parties. You would agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I agree with that e-mail Mr. President; it's just that particularly with regard to paragraph 2 page 1, the fact that if we could just move to page 1 the fact that it is left there, even if Mr. Misetic is going to lead live, I wonder how that is going to -- what kind of impact has because if Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait and see what questions Mr. Misetic will put to the witness and then he will be better able to see whether we have to consider any impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may comment, Your Honour. Not 15 minutes ago Ms. Mahindaratne took paragraph 5 of her supplemental statement read it to the witness first and then that is how she had led it life so I'm not sure -- I'm following exactly the course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you indicated that do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed at this moment, we'll see what happens, and then the Chamber will respond if there's any need to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if we could please have on the screen Exhibit P973, please. Your Honour, should we get a MFI number first for the Defence witness statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar. Not only a MFI. I think there was no objection. Let me see whether we did already and we admitted it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one to one now on admission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Trying to keep up. Page 10 of the English version, Mr. Registrar. I don't know -- perhaps Ms. Mahindaratne knows the B/C/S page of ... there we go. The entry at 1720, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, you were asked by the Prosecution yesterday - it's to the left on the bottom - about this entry at 1720 on the 10th of August. You were asked some questions about a order that had been received in the mail and says it's an order to comply with military disciplinary measures from the command of the Military District Split. Do you recall being questioned about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to pay particular attention to the class and delivery number, okay? And what I'm going to show you now first is Exhibit D204, Mr. Registrar. As you can see, there is an order from General Gotovina on the 10th of August, the same day as the entry in the log-book, and it's an order -- it says: "In order to prevent theft of property, undisciplined conduct and to save human lives," and then there's order there from General Gotovina. You can read through that. And at the bottom it says - if we could scroll down in the English, please, or go to the next page, apologise - it says it is delivered to Operative Group Zapad, Operative Group Sibenik." Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D56-0048 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the commander of Operative Group Sibenik that was received in the 113th brigade received the same day in which the commander of Operative Group Sibenik is passing on the order he has received from General Gotovina if you look at the bottom left-hand corner which should be page 2, I guess, in the -- It says it is delivered to the -- the fourth entry says 4/72nd battalion of the military police - for information. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go back to the header on the first page in English, if you look at the class number and the reference number, that reference number and that class number match the numbers that are found in the log-book of the 4th Company of the 72nd MP Battalion. So it would appear that this is the order that arrived in the mail on the 10th. And my question to you, sir, is when it says, "for information to the 4th Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion that is not an order to them, is it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why does a commander send to the military police orders on information?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to keep them abreast of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked that Exhibit 1D56 --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Preside, I object to that. I don't know from where Mr. Misetic gathered that this is not an order. The document reads at the top as an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Misetic is dealing with is to whom this order was addressed. That apparently is the issue, and we have heard the answer of the witness. The Chamber can read the document. And Mr. Misetic paid specific attention to the fact that at the bottom of this document it was said that it was send for information to the 4th Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. That's how I understand the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against admission, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D841.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D841 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have on the screen, please, Exhibit D269. And if we could go to paragraph number 2, which is page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the head of the military police administration, General Lausic, right on the eve of Operation Storm. And if we look at section 2. If could you read that please. I'm putting this to you because you were asked some questions earlier today as to how the military police was to handle civilians? This was the order issued by General Lausic to the military police on that issue. If could you read through that and then we'll move on to section 3 when you're finished.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to the next page, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's just paragraph 3 that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before today, have you ever seen this order before?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that you're a military policeman, was this order intended to deal with the issue of civilians in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object to that, Mr. President, what is the foundation for this witness to be able to give an interpretation to document he has never seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If that is the standard, Your Honour, then I think the Prosecution's direct examination could be shortened greatly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now and then foundation is asked and it would not be a bad idea to do the same here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the military police -- do you know if there's an issue in a combat zone, sir, that when you enter a combat zone there are civilians that may be there?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And during the course of combat action in the military police, generally speaking, would the military police receive instructions as to how civilians in a combat zone should be treated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And would civilians in a combat zone, from your experience, be taken to a safer area so that they wouldn't be in a combat zone any longer?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To make sure that they are not in danger, they would be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your response to Ms. Mahindaratne earlier on this question you did say you thought it was maybe because -- that civilians were taken to collection officers for their safety. Would this order be consistent with your understanding as to why civilians would be taken to collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Objection Mr. President the witness has not seen this document and his testimony is clear he has never received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has now seen this, and he is asked whether this is consistent with his understanding of what his or the military police duty was at that time, which is a -- an admissible question. Please proceed. The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If civilians are found to be present in combat areas, particularly children, women, and the elderly, but all of the civilians they have to be placed somewhere safely -- placed away somewhere safely because their place of residence is in danger due to ongoing combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic briefly before the break. Mr. Registrar, 1D56-0043, please. Just to draw the Court's attention this is a document that I'm putting to the witness that addresses an issue raised earlier this week between myself and Mr. Margetts regarding an incident at a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a report of the military police in Benkovac from the 19th of September, 1995. And I'd ask you to take a look at it, and I'd just like to ask you a few questions about it. It concerns an incident at a check-point regarding a HV officer who had been stopped by the Croatian civilian police and had his rear tire shot out. This is the military police's version of that event.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read the extent I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you what you've read up to this point. Based on your experience as a military policeman, the check-point that is referenced here, is that a joint check-point between the military police and the MUP; or is that a MUP check-point and the military police were called in as a result of an incident?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, it was not stated that this was a joint check-point. The military police team came from Zadar, and I seem to be familiar with these persons judging by their names, in order to carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this incident?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As far as you know from your service in the military police, was the -- the Croatian civilian police authorised to use force against a member of the Croatian army if it was necessary in order to prevent him from continuing in committing a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to act according to their powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did those powers include the ability to use force to stop a member of the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender into evidence 1D56-0043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D842.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D842 is admitted into evidence. Yes, we're looking at the clock. At the same time, could the parties assist me in telling me where even if the witness doesn't know where Obonjan Island is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can ask my client, Your Honour, if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He might be the only one in the room that knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course we could check that on the map. Of the accused are not invited to give evidence, but at the same time this might --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Obonjan Island is just across the town of Sibenik, and it is a well known touristic destination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see what I can -- because I would have one follow-up question before we go to the -- before we have a break. You were asked whether moving out the elderly would be consistent with taking them to a safe place. Could you tell us, when did you consider the actual combat situation to be not directly endangering the civilian population anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the answer to that. I can't gauge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Operation Storm took place, 4th, 5th of August, by the 10th of August, would the combat operations be such that there was still a need to move civilians from areas where combat could be expected or was taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible. If there were skirmishes, the situation may have been threatening and endangering them at the time as well. I don't know. I was not out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if it was the task of the military police to bring them to a safe place, you would have to know, isn't it, when there was a need to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clarify the following. I was heading the military police crime service. I did not take part in the activities on the ground. I did not tour the check-points. That's why I'm not familiar with such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware of the reception officer for civilians, which was mentioned in the document that was shown to you earlier? Did you know about the existence of that reception centre for civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you consider that a safe place for civilians at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so. It was outside of any -- of reach of any combat activities at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it consistent with bringing civilians to a safe place to drive them out of this reception centre and to take them to another reception centre on the island of Obonjan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that was in -- in order. That was all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if they are in a safe place, you are free to move them to another safe place, on an island, perhaps further away from home. Was it your understanding that you were free to move these civilians even though in a safe place, to other safe places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my knowledge, Baldekin was the reception centre for both civilians and prisoners of war. Of course prisoners of war had to be separated from civilians, and thus civilians were being taken to a safer reception centre by being transported do the Obonjan island.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At that point in time, which is the -- I think it was the 12th of August. There was still a need to bring them to a safer place. It was not safe enough in the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that it was not safe, but there was no need for them to be there at Baldekin that was in the centre of town, and there was no need for them to be placed together with prisoners of war, if there were any at the time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We'll have a break. We'll resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you asked permission to briefly address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I we would just like on behalf of all three defense teams some -- just to put on the record and ask for the trial chambers guidance, but we think there may be some confusion about these collection centres, and I'm not asking for an answer now but if there is further submission that the Trial Chamber wants on this issue, where they were, et cetera, our position with respect to the two specific centres that were questioning him about before, where they were moved from a basketball court to luxury hotels is essentially what transpired there. But we try to deal with that issue with Mr. Kardum but if the chamber wants further submissions on this, I think all three Defence teams are prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll keep it in the back of our minds whether basketball fields or other locations at what point in time would give greater safety. That's good that it's on the record. If we need it, we will certainly ask for it. And then perhaps, Ms. Mahindaratne, if it would be joint submissions, the Chamber would even prefer that. Then anything else? Not. Then may the witness be --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- brought into the courtroom against. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think P967, 968, 969 are still in MFI status. If I'm not mistaken, they were not admitted into evidence. Those are the three statements, Mr. President. The statement of 28 January -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- no, it was two statements and a letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they have now been uploaded. And the letter was already admitted into evidence. Isn't it? Because there was no redaction needed there. Whereas the two statements, that January statement and the October statement, they had to be uploaded, redacted, and as we saw them being uploaded, that is in accordance with the agreement. So therefore I take it that there's no objection against admission anymore. Mr. Registrar, the -- could you repeat the numbers I think it is P967, P968 are now admitted into evidence, whereas P969, the letter, was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And also, Mr. President, P972, now all translations are uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, all the chapters you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the Defence could verify that that's the case, and therefore no further objections, then, it's ready to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, P9 -- no, I'm now making a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P972 is admitted into evidence. With the relevant cover page and the relevant pages -- the relevant chapters being translated whereas the original is the full document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have on the screen Exhibit P974.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is the monthly report that we've talked about yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of this report, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the report that you sent, it talks about in the last sentence it says: "In the above-mentioned time-period, members of the Sibenik crime investigation military police filed nine reports for violation of military discipline. Who did the military crime police file such reports with?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the brigades that the perpetrators were members of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And would the military police receive information back once any disciplinary measure was taken?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was up to the commander of any such unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The military police had a role, however, in -- in keeping commanders informed about breaches of military discipline. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours with your permission I would like to use some words in Croatian here and have the translators assist me with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To a limited extent to help us out, but it should really be the exception because that's not their task, and if there is any issue remaining it should be dealt with by CLSS by the -- by the translators not by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One sentence in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you know the difference between a disciplinary or breach of discipline or an act of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreter -- could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer in full because the interpreters could not translate it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us the difference between a breach of discipline or a disciplinary offence and act of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A breach of discipline is a graver offence, and a disciplinary is measure is something that is issued by commander. And this is a minor offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, from the answer I take it there may be confusion. Could I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's actually an issue I've been trying to figure out for awhile now on how to translate those words because they're extremely difficult to translate into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would try to put the question into English and see -- you also could ask him whether he --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could perhaps ask the witness a more open question on whether he knows different forms of -- different forms of not meeting the requirements of discipline. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, there are really under the Croatian system at the time two different types of breaches of discipline. One is a so-called minor infraction of discipline, such as failure to keep your boots tied; failure to keep your uniform tidy; failure to keep your bed neat. And then there are serious violations of military discipline. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to serious violations of military discipline, can you describe for us, first of all, what you would consider to be a serious violation of military discipline?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would be violations that in -- put life in danger or that would put property in danger, and such instances were dealt with by the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was there also something in the Croatian system known as the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And it existed specifically for such cases as we have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if someone, a Croatian army soldier, committed a serious breach of military discipline, that soldier would be brought before the military disciplinary court to determine whether he should be punished for that breach of discipline. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the report that we have on the screen, was that a report that you sent to your superior, Mr. Boris Milas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you have already testified that Boris Milas was the chief of the crime -- military crime police at the level of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. Are you aware that his superior was the chief of the crime police in Zagreb at the military police administration, a gentleman by the name of Spomenko Eljuga?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could be please repeat the name of the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: S-p-o-m-e-n-k-o, E-l-j-u-g-a.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, are you correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Milas passed on your report to the military police administration in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his duty to compile the reports that he received from all the battalions and refer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. From all the companies and refer that compiled report to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I insisted earlier on knowing what happens rather than what duties were, so could you please also for the following questions try to find out what happened, not only what people were duty-bound to do. Here is the answer -- you asked him whether it was -- I think whether the report was passed, and the answer was he was duty-bound to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this particular report was ever sent by Mr. Milas to Zagreb, either as it is or as part of a -- part of a compilation report that he would send to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
