utterances.text: Maybe not in this form. However, the figures and the tables were enclosed with the report that he did sent to Zagreb. When we're talking about information, and I mean figures, tables that was sent to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if, in the military police administration in Zagreb, they were the ones that were to review the work that had been completed for that month, meaning August 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. This is above my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the case of Goran Vunic. Now Goran Vunic was a commander in the HV. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was the commander of a reconnaissance platoon in a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So in the fall of 1995, you were authorised to investigate commanders who were involved in criminal activity. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the military crime police determined that a commander of a unit was complicit in a crime, what steps would you have had to take?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in case of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Which would mean what?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a crime was committed, the crime was identified, qualified, and all the necessary documents were collected and sent to the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that you were ordered by Commander Mrkota to stop the investigation of Mr. Vunic. Did you advise your superior, Mr. Milas, that Commander Mrkota had ordered you to stop the investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you've testified today that you were acting pursuant to a search warrant that had been issued by a Court. Did you ever -- did the Court ever inquire of you at some point as to whether you had actually executed the warrant?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar if we could have on the screen 1D56-0001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that perhaps I could ask one additional question. Mr. Simic, earlier you were asked about disciplinary violations of discipline and -- and crimes and about disciplinary court. Now looting, could looting ever be a disciplinary contravention or a disciplinary misbehaviour rather than a crime? Would it be dealt with under disciplinary law, rather than under criminal law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A criminal report submitted against a perpetrator did not exclude a disciplinary measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could it ever be considered to be a disciplinary contravention, or whatever word I should use, and dealt with as such and not as a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If theft indeed happened and if the perpetrators -- perpetrator was caught, a criminal report would be filed, and if this was not the case, then the measure applied would be a disciplinary measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to understand what you exactly say, is that if no criminal report would be filed, it could be dealt with through disciplinary measures. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think you earlier told us that you wouldn't know whether crime reports would always be made in respect of such cases. Does that mean that you also do not know to what extent looting was dealt with as -- in terms of disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Before we get to this document, Baldekin, are you familiar with what Baldekin is in Sibenik, B-a-l-d-e-k-i-n?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baldekin is a sports hall, a basketball hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is that where the civilians were taken in the initial days of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now on the screen, sir. This is a judgement concerning the case that you had investigated. And we've translated certain excerpts. In the judgement, you can see that Goran Vunic subsequently became a witness in that case and gave evidence as a witness. Were you aware subsequent to October 1995 that Goran Vunic became a witness in the case that you had investigated?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we move into private session just for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- we've excerpted only the relevant portions of the judgement, so I would tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, with judgements what is relevant and what is not relevant of course, Ms. Mahindaratne, have you been in a position to form an opinion about the selection made by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to just this excerpt in because I'm familiar with the document, and I think the entire document we ourselves intended to submit this document later on from the bar table so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you already -- is there already a translation of the whole of the document available?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: At that stage I'm not aware as to whether we have a -- may I just inquire from the -- my team and get back to you, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I do understand that you have no objection against the introduction into evidence of this judgement, but you'd rather have the whole of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just advise the Court, OTP has chunks translated but not the entire document translated. We've taken from their chunks a smaller chunk. I have no objection to the whole judgement coming in either, but for purposes of when we have to deal with this at the end of the day, I think it might be easier if the reference so Goran Vunic are easily accessible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited to agree on those portions of the judgement that they both consider not to be relevant for this case and then to have the remainder tendered into evidence. I think since the original is a complete document, I take it, then we already assign a number to that. It will be marked for identification, and we'll wait what the parties agree upon as relevance of all portions of it. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number D843, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It keeps that status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could we please have on the screen, Exhibit D267.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is an order from General Lausic dated 2 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go in the English, please, to page 4, and in the Croatian it is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a General Lausic's order, and in the second paragraph in section 10, he says that he: "Appoints Major Ivan Juric and a group of officers from the regular VP section and the VP administration crime section to assist in commanding and organizing the activities of the 72nd VP Battalion, and 73rd VP Battalion that shall perform tasks in its own area of responsibility and provide necessary assistance to the 72nd VP Battalion?" And then the sentence: "The commanders of the 72nd VP Battalion and 73rd VP Battalion shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Exhibit D268, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a follow-up order referencing the order we just read, and it says -- if we could go to the next page in English, please. It's the 3rd of August, 1995. The introduction says: "Pursuant to the assessed and demonstrated need with a view to efficient and effective implementation of military police and other tasks in VP units' zones of responsibility, and effective system of command, supervision, and provision of professional assistance to RHOS VP units, I hereby issue the following order." And section one says: "A group of UVP officers led by major Ivan Juric including the following officers: Senior lieutenant Damir Muduna from the UVP department, senior lieutenant Ante Glavan." Now do you know who Ante Glavan?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Who was that on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the crime police department attached to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your activities in the field during and after Operation Storm, did you ever come across Ante Glavan?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once in Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Was it related to military police duties?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How about Major Ivan Juric, did you ever come across him during or after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Sibenik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And how many times did you see him in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as was the case with Ante Glavan. They were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you describe for us the circumstances of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came to visit the barracks where the 4th Company was billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what transpired there? Did they do a review of your work?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They attended a meeting with the company commander. They were there probably for agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any information was provided to them about the results of the work of the crime military police section of the 4th Company during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 423.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by General Lausic. It appears that it is issued and addressed directly to the 3rd Company, 4th Company and 6th Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. It does not appear to go through either Major Juric or Mr. Budimir but goes directly from Mr. Lausic to your company. Now, please take a look and read through this document. At least the first page of it. Actually, to save some time, I will take you to the relevant portion the first is the subject. On the second page, we see that this was received 4 August 1995 and dispatched 4 August. The subject is: "Contents of reports in relation to the performance of the military police tasks as per the order of the chief of the military police administration." In point 12 it said that Mr. Juric was obligated to sent reports to the military police administration everyday by 8.00 p.m. And then General Lausic following up on that point, issues this order on what those reports -- what information those reports need to contain. In the introduction it says the report is to be submitted directly to the MP administration by using code system. If we go to paragraph number 2. It says: "The content of the report shall contain, 2, the status of public law and order, in a zone of combat operations, and in newly liberated areas, stating events when the MP had to act and results of intervention." Point 4: "The status of crime in liberated areas and in zones of combat operations. Number of crimes, crime reports filed and escort of HV members who committed a crime." And then we go to point 9: "The system of daily reporting through services remains as it is. This report is to be signed by a MP unit commander, that is, officers of the MP administration in accordance with the item 12 of the above-mentioned order, starting with 4 August 1995, and including the status at 1900 hours." Now, in point 9 the officer of the MP administration as we see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the witness might be confused by not finding a number 9 on his document because after 8 although it continues, there's no 9. Where it is in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's the paragraph which begin, Mr. Simic, after the paragraph number 8. Now, the officer of the MP administration referenced in item 12 is Mr. Juric. So this order goes directly from General Lausic to your company. Do you recall sending information to Major Juric concerning the number of crime, crimes reports filed, and escort of HV members who committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember sending any reports to him. We sent daily reports to the duty service, which sent them on to the HQ of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if the commander of the 4th Company of the 72 Military Police Battalion received an order directly from General Lausic, and in that order the commander of the company needs to provide or is ordered to provide information about the number of crimes -- crime reports filed, and escort of HV members who committed a crime, the commander of the 4th Company presumably would have had to go to you as the head of the crime police section in the 4th Company to obtain those -- that information. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that, since I sent daily reports to the duty service. He was able to find the information he needed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I add that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D844.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D844 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have on the screen 1D56-0051.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now a report from Commander Mrkota, the commander of the 4th Company reporting to the commander of the 72nd MP Battalion on the 7th of August and he says in the opening paragraph : "Pursuant to the oral order of the chief of the military police administration, Major-General Mate Lausic, received 7 August 1995 at 1310 hours, who ordered that a security system be established urgently at the entries and exits of the following warehouses," and then it goes on. Were you aware at that time during and after Operation Storm that General Lausic was issuing orders directly to the commander of the 4th Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in your experience unusual about General Lausic issuing orders to a company in the military police battalion that did not go through the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the chain of command was interrupted this way, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked that these be marked, and I tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D845.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D845 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive an order from any HV officer -- directly receive an order from any HV officer who was not himself a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions about your background, Mr. Simic. What level of police training do you have?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've mostly attended courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what type of courses you took prior to being appointed the head of the crime military police of the 4th Company?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I was not a chief. I was merely at the head of the service. The chief was Boris Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It may be -- I said head of the crime military police of the 4th Company. So can you tell us what type of courses you took before you were appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drugs abuse course; peacekeeping operations course. I believe that those were the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You didn't receive any type of training in criminal -- criminal investigative work. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you were the head of that section in -- sorry. The head of the crime police, military police section in the 4th Company although had you no prior training in criminal investigative work?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now a few basic questions. You had a legal duty to investigate any crime that was committed by a member of the HV in your area of responsibility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If the offence was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: With the exception of your investigation of Goran Vunic, were you ever told not to investigate a criminal act committed by a member of the HV?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Save for the specific offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood that last part. What do you mean by, "save for the specific offence"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none other than the Goran Vunic case, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the military police has information that a crime has been committed by a member of the HV what is the job of the military police at that point?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the duty to take all measures to investigate the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If, for some reason, you are obstructed in your ability to conduct a criminal investigation, whether it's because the commander of a particular unit is interfering with your work, or you are shorthanded, what steps do you take if there is some inability on your part to conduct that criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would draw up a written report stating the reasons why I cannot do that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And can the witnesses repeat the last thing he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the last portion of your answer Mr. Simic. The interpreter didn't hear you. And if you could speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I would make written reports about the reasons why I could not conduct the investigation, and I would orally report to my reporters about the matter -- to my superiors about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you would make a written report, who would you send the written report to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally the reports would remain part of the case file. That was the case when Goran Vunic was concerned. I made a written report about why I would not carry out the investigation and I orally reported to my superior, Boris Milas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, is there a reason that you would orally report that obstruction in your investigation rather than filing a written report to your superior?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no reason behind that. Reports can be submitted orally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, how would you -- how would you later be able to document the fact that you alerted your superior to the fact that you had been interfered with in an investigation? For example --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically only the Official Note, such as I made in the Goran Vunic case. If we're talking about that specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you -- not necessarily talking about that specific case. But how would you prove to someone later that you alerted your superior to the fact that there had been some sort of interference in your ability to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a specific situation where it was impossible to submit a written report. Normally one does put it on paper as well, to have some trace of it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have Exhibit P203 on the Krajina again please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, meanwhile I would like to seek a clarification of the last answer. You said, "This was a specific situation where it was impossible to submit a written report." What made it impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you a specific answer. It may have been the workload or my absence from the unit. There could have been a number of reasons. It was a busy time, and plenty of duties to do, attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your previous answer was not under the prevailing circumstances it might have been difficult. You said: "It was a specific situation where it was impossible to submit a written report." What made the situation so specific that it was impossible to write a written report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Perhaps I didn't explain it in my first answer, but I did in the second. That was it. The specificity of the situation consisted in the great work loud, busy schedule, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were shown this document earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to the bottom portion in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again a report on the 8th of August that talks about the fact that in the areas of Bribirski Mostine, Djevrska, and Kistanje, the situation is rather chaotic. Incidents of mass burning houses, plundering of property, alcohol consumption occur, and units lack organisation. Then the second-to-last sentence says: "A military police platoon has been assigned to the area in order to normalise the situation concerning the HV members."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to P973, Mr. Registrar, please, and page 6 in the English of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now this document on the 8th refers to a platoon that was sent to Kistanje on the 6th -- sorry, that was sent to Kistanje to normalise the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we go again to the log-book of the 4th Company. If we could go to the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At 2050, on the 6th of August, the 4th Company's log-book identifies the military policemen that went he to Kistanje. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So on the 6th we have an entry that the members of the platoon were sent to Kistanje. On the 8th, there's confirmation that they were sent to normalise the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to D737, please. If we could go to page 9 in the English of this document. Actually, I'm sorry, page 4 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report of Commander Budimir that goes to Mr. Lausic on the 13th of August, 1995. If you look on page 4 you'll note that it does not go to the Split Military District but only goes to Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 9 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And at the bottom of that page in English, there's an entry there at the bottom that says that: "The first platoon of the military police ..." I should take a step back. This is the section of the report that talks about the 4th Company from Sibenik. It says: "The first platoon of the military police and their 24 military policemen have been relocated to Kistanje. Now, my first -- it appears that military police were in Kistanje. My next question to you, sir, is are you aware that Major Ivan Juric was himself in Kistanje during this period between the 4th of August and the time of the filing of this report?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we go to D274, please. This is page 4 in the English version; page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is from a diary of a UN military policeman. And in it, towards the bottom, he says: "Driving towards Benkovac, met Ivan ..." And he has already testified that that means Ivan Juric. "... on the road and said, hi. He said he was going around to lots of places. Asked if we could follow. Said yes. Went to a couple of places. We waited while he talked to people. Stopped at a factory, east side of Kistanje. He went in, about 12 military policemen." Now, that is a report of a UN military policeman on the 9th of August placing Mr. Juric in Kistanje with the platoon of the 4th Company that had been dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go now to D732 for Mr. Juric's report to Mr. Lausic for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the report, which presumably is issued to the orders that we've already gone through by General Lausic to have Mr. Juric report to him about criminal activity that is taking place --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, presumably, I don't know on what basis, you know -- I don't think presumption what we -- is required in this proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I won't presume then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I established the orders and unless Ms. Mahindaratne knows of some other order to Mr. Juric concerning reporting I would suggest that those are the orders he is acting under.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is a matter Mr. President's Trial Chamber will address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to avoid as much as possible all kind of presumptions in questions, although I do see there's a greater margin for the Defence in cross-examining a Prosecution witness than there would be for the Prosecution when examining in chief their own witnesses. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Major Juric was issued an order on the 3rd of August to report to the military police station -- military police administration about acts of criminal activity and what measures were being taken. On the 9th of August, he is seen in Kistanje with the MP platoon. And for that day, there's no mention in the report about any problems in Kistanje, or any action being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next day, which is D733.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And will you note that Major Juric's reports go only to the military police administration. Point 2: "The 4th Sibenik Company area of responsibility, in addition to their regular military police tasks, the members of this unit are still guarding two industrial facilities and the Orthodox monastery in Kistanje." There's no additional information about any action being taken by the military police in Kistanje on the 10th. Now, I put it to you that we've seen orders now from General Lausic both -- on the 2nd, the 3rd as well as an order that he issued directly to the 4th Company of the military police requiring that information on a daily basis concerning criminal activity be sent to him by 8.00 p.m. if there was information in the possession of the 4th Company that a crime had been committed in Kistanje, that information should have been included in Mr. Juric's reports. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If measures were being taken to conduct a criminal investigation into criminal activity that took place in Kistanje, that information should have been in the reports that Major Juric was sending to General Lausic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how it transpired that the 4th Company of Sibenik was in Kistanje and that Major Juric was in Kistanje and that --

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain. This was not what I was dealing with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, why -- and I was going to say and Ante Glavan who you identified as the person who went with Major Juric into the field and who was from the crime police section in the administration in Zagreb, how it is that you never received a call to come to Kistanje and conduct a criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I we've seen the exhibit. I don't need to show you anymore about eight crimes having been solved in August 1995. That averages out -- you also testified yesterday that you had eight men under your -- at your disposal; let's put it that way. How is it that in one month, on average, you -- your men were able to solve one crime each?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the crime, and the nature of the crime, whether it was a complicated or a simple crime. I could not set the pace. The employees themselves determined how fast they could work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the question that arose yesterday and that I will put to you, to give you an opportunity to explain, is if, on average, each -- each person solved one crime, tell the Court what it is that they were doing with the rest of their time.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they were working on some other investigations that had already started before. In any case, they were not idle. Some investigations took months, a month, month and a half. It took time to collect all the material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Invite the witness to be concrete on these matters. You say it may be that they were working on other cases. Could you give us information about the eight men, not a huge number, which were at your disposal. Tell us a case which they were working on which took them a month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe they were collecting evidence that was not readily available. It was not their fault that they could not get hold of the evidence immediately. Maybe there were other services involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming them. What I would like you to do is to give us one case, not what they maybe have done, but give us one case in which they were engaged in investigations for a month in that period of time. Must have been a major case if it takes you a month and keeps you busy instead of paying attention to other matters. Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you the example of members of the 7th Guards Brigade from Osijek. When that brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm talking about your eight people, no one else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I'm trying to tell you. At that moment there were not eight people because six -- two were in Drnis, so we're talking about six people, myself and five others. But members of the 7th Guards Brigade had committed a crime and certain evidence was collected. But then that brigade or at least some members of it withdrew into the barracks, so it was more difficult to collect all necessary information. Maybe some of the material had to undergo a forensic expertise. I don't know why the investigation could not be completed in a short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What crime had they committed, these members of the 7th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If one of your subordinates committed a disciplinary infraction, did you have the authority to discipline him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the company commander, Nenad Mrkota, who had that authority. But also he had to accompany that with a report to Major Boris.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of military policemen themselves being disciplined or criminally prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any instance in the four years between 1991 and 1995 when a military policeman received a disciplinary measure?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some mild disciplinary measures for inappropriate behaviour or some such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Who could issue disciplinary measures to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander. The company commander would issue a proposal and then the battalion commander would order the measure that was previously already identified by the company commander. What I'm say something is that the company commander would issue a proposal and accompany it with a proposal of the measure that was to be instituted, and then the battalion commander would either accept the suggestion or reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If there was some problem in the work of the crime police section, isn't it the case that the action was to be taken by Mr. Milas and then, above him, by the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any instance where an HV commander who was not in the military police could discipline or otherwise remove someone who was within the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. I suggest that we have a break now. May I take it that the estimates given yesterday have not grown overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They've changed, in the sense that the content has -- has had to change because of developments today. I will try and keep to the half another I said, but I think it is more likely to be 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the other side, Your Honour, I will have no cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No cross. That -- Then we will have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Ms. Mahindaratne, could I already inquire with you, whether you have a lot of question in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So far only five questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you will you now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if we could just look at your statement that you made in January 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit P967, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just look at the first paragraph. And I'm going to ask you some questions about the commander of the 72nd. If we look at your statement here, we see that you refer to Colonel Budimir, Mihael Budimir as being the commander of the 72nd. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You just looked at some documents about half an hour ago concerning Major Juric and we saw some orders from General Lausic actually appointing him the commander of the 72nd from the 3rd of August, 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So this paragraph here should be amended, shouldn't it, to reflect that fact, that during the period from the 3rd of August, 1995 afterwards, Major Juric was the commander of the 72nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President. I object, Mr. President. The witness was shown documents. This is his testimony, and it is up to the parties to present the evidence to the Trial Chamber and ask for a conclusion on this matter, not ask the witness to change his statement according to the material that is shown to him in the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The evidence given by the witness can be tested in cross-examination and that could include that matters are put to him either the same matters or other matters and that questions are asked and then we'll see whether the witness gives the same answers or whether he will clarify or will further detail whatever he earlier testified. You may proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Am I right Mr. Simic, that in this paragraph here it should be amended to reflect the fact that Major Juric was the commander of the 72nd Battalion for a period of time in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information Mihael Budimir was the commander and Mr. Juric was the coordinator of certain operations or actions that I'm not aware of or familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you notice in those orders you looked at today that it said that Major Juric was the commander of the 72nd and the 73rd.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Mr. Lausic's rapporteur from the field. I suppose he had authorities, but I don't know what those were. I don't know what powers he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Also looking at this paragraph here, it says that your commander was Captain Mrkota, and you received orders from Captain Mrkota who, in turn, received his orders from Budimir?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've also told us today that, in fact, you received orders from Boris Milas who was head of the criminal section of the 72nd. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that you received orders from Major Boris Milas of the criminal section, and you reported to Boris Milas of the criminal section?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your statement here in paragraph 1, whilst being accurate concerning Captain Mrkota and Colonel Budimir, would you agree, doesn't show the full reporting and subordination chain of the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at paragraph 3 of the statement you have here, you refer to the 72nd Battalion consisting of an anti-terrorist platoon, nine general military police companies, and you name them: Sinj, the next one, Gospic. Wasn't Gospic not part of the 72nd but, in fact, a company of the 71st?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So the paragraph here is also inaccurate in this statement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the 71st Battalion. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 71st Battalion of the military police Gospic was subordinated to the 72nd Battalion which was probably under the command of Aladzic [phoen] but it was on the strength of the 71st military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's just look at the rest of the companies there. Knin, Sibenik, Zadar, Split, and then Metkovic. Wasn't that a platoon under the Dubrovnik company?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubrovnik had a company as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Metkovic was not one of the companies of the 72nd Battalion, was it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Metkovic was a military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And would I be right in saying it was a platoon under the Dubrovnik command?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know under whose command it was, but it was certainly a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. So this part of your statement here is -- is wrong as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is actually complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next name, Makarska. That wasn't one of the companies of the 72nd, was it? That was also a platoon.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a company. It was a platoon; you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so would you agree your statement should be amended on that matter as well?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to Split, were there two companies that made up the battalion from Split, one a combat military police company, and the other a general military police company?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would add to that that there was also a traffic police company, in addition to the two that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. A traffic company. But I was interested in pointing out that Split actually had two companies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it had three companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you include the traffic as part of it -- one of the Split companies?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just look at a organigram please. If the Court could produce 2D06-0020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you a diagram here - it can be put into your language there for you; it's also in the English language - of the commanding and reporting in relation to the 72nd Battalion. Shall we just look at the bottom line first where we've seen the company, first of all, the 1st Company, that was from Split. That is right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then the 2nd Company next to that from Split. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 3rd Company, Zadar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your company, the 4th, Sibenik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 5th is the Sinj company. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 6th, Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then we've got the 7th, which is the Knin company. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then we've got the traffic company, the 3rd one, from Split, That you wanted to tell me about? Have I got the companies right there, for the companies that make up the 72nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've got them right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can see a box at the bottom which has the criminal section of the military police next to the Sibenik 4th Company, and there your name is, because you were part of the 4th. Is that right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see a bold arrow going up, connecting you to the criminal section of the military police where the chief was Major Milas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that you were subordinated to Major Milas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that the -- all the companies of the 72nd were subordinated to Colonel Budimir who was the commander of the 72nd. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that also included the criminal section under Major Milas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But Major Milas actually reported on his work line to Captain Eljuga, if you follow the arrow from his box who was part of the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And he was the chief of the military police crime department within the military police administration over which General Lausic was the chief. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the other squads, platoons of the 72nd. I'm just going to ask you some questions now about those boxes on the second from top line, where Captain Eljuga was. And within the military police administration next to Captain Eljuga's box, we see Major Juric, Major Ivan Juric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that the Major Juric we're talking about who came down to be in the Knin region with the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that all those lines reported up to General Lausic, who was the chief of the administration for the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your work, down at the bottom of the diagram again, we're going back down to where you are at the foot of it, did your orders in relation to your criminal police work come from Major Milas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the system was that as a member of the criminal section of the 72nd, you were attached to the 4th Company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not attached. We were on the establishment of the 4th Company. The criminal section was on the establishment of the 4th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document go into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. For the record, I understand that this is organigram prepared by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understand it as well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hope there's nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number D846.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D846, nothing wrong with that, but good to have it on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's, then, have a look, as I know Your Honour likes to see it in action, the reporting lines. I'd like us to look, first of all, at a document, and I'm revising my cross-examination, Your Honour, in view of my learned friend's earlier cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Document 65 ter 1002. It is P978 now. Exhibit P978.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this is a document you looked at yesterday dated the 7th of August, 1995. And it concerns the 72nd and the 4th Company. And on the 7th of August, this was send to Major Juric. And if we look at the last page of the English - but it's on the same page of the Croatian version - by your commander, Captain Mrkota. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... see Captain Mrkota's name at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you'll notice that this is sent to Major Juric. And it's information with regard to the implementation of military police tasks pursuant to the OVP commander's order. What does OVP stand for?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UVP is the military police administration. And OVP stands for the military police department, or section ... I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There's an error in the way that it has been written in the English where it has got O instead of U. It's UVP. So this reporting line from Captain Mrkota, the commander of the 4th, was pursuant to the military police administration commander's order, and that is General Lausic, isn't it, commander of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so this report from Captain Mrkota to Major Juric, on his tasks, is as a result of the military police administration commander's order. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've no need to go further into the detail of that because I note time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document I would like to look at, please, is 65 ter 2972.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 22nd of August, 1995. It's one send by you, Mr. Simic, on that date, from the 4th Company to the military police administration crime investigation department, to its chief, Boris Milas. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your name is on the second page of the English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the second page can be put onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And there you are. Do you recollect sending this document to Mr. Milas?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that this was a routine document that you send him?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just reporting to him on matters concerning the reception centre in Sibenik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 641 -- oh, can I make that an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D847, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D847 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 641, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 18th of August, 1995. It comes from the 3rd Company, this time of the military police, the Zadar Company. And it's sent by them to Major Milas, erroneously described in that draft translation as a brigadier. And it's a report to him concerning people in the collection centre. And if we just look at page 2 in the English and page 2 in the Croatian document, you'll see it's signed by the head of the crime police, Captain Babic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would it be right to say that he was in charge of the crime police within the Zadar Company of the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And like you sent your report to Major Milas, would you describe this as being a routine report to him about a matter at the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, let's first proceed with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. D848 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay I'm seeking your assistance. You earlier talked about the report on prisoners of war. I think it is the first time that you said is this a routine report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will remember that earlier there was some discussion about collection centres and basketball grounds. I think it was the same centre where there was the issue of five people being there, 80 people taken out whether it was one or -- Now, the document says that the full list of those detained is attached. It's not part of the document. Is the attachment to that document also available? Because it might shed some light not on the issue you're raising but one of the issues we dealt with earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it had been there we would have uploaded it obviously because -- it's from the Prosecution's 65 ter list and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is there any way to verify and to check whether this would bring us any further in relation to the other matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll have -- I will have to have someone check that the 65 ter number -- or, I mean, just because it is from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I help -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The B/C/S version as I have just been told, the Croatian version has all the names. It's the English language version that does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's not translated. We can check that, whether it is already done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a practice often where there are lists of names that those translating don't set out the whole list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is true that where the English translation is a two-page document, the original is ten-page document, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the Court will be able to look at the Croatian attachment, probably serve its purposes. But if it does need further work, perhaps the Court would let the parties know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think at least what we find is certainly a lot of date of birth, and we'll have a look at it to see whether we need further assistance from the parties to interpret that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, do I that I can the document with the attachment goes in as -- and the exhibit or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is how it was uploaded. Nevertheless, the Chamber would highly appreciate if the translation is not covering the complete document, that at least we are aware of that, so that not by looking at the English translation with think that that's all what is in evidence, but that there is more. And I do agree that lists of names usually are not very helpful, but sometimes the titles in the columns may assist us, first of all, in being aware that there is more; and, second, to understand the originals. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we look at 65 ter 2648.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is a document, Mr. Simic, dated the 2nd of October, 1995. It's again from the Zadar Company. And it's from Captain Babic, the head of the crime police of the Zadar Company. And it is send to the 72nd, crime investigation section, which is Major Milas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't really focusing on your question. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, it's from the 3rd Company, Zadar. If you look at to whom it is addressed, it is addressed to the 72nd crime investigation section to the section chief, that's Major Milas. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm not interested in the content of the report because that is not what I'm dealing with at this stage. And you can see handwritten, if the Croatian version could be brought down, please, so that we look at the handwriting on -- on the top. That Major Milas has sent this to Captain Spomenko Eljuga who was in charge of the crime police in the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And also beneath that from the military police administration, the name of Brigadier Biskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on our organigram we looked at a moment ago, we know that Brigadier Biskic is second in command to General Lausic of the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you agree that this shows the reporting line within the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's a document there that doesn't have to go to Colonel Budimir who, at this time, was the commander of the 72nd. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 72nd military police crime investigation section had a direct line, that they could go up to the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look -- may we make this an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D849 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 2170 Spomenko Eljuga?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we're now going to look at two documents from Major Milas where he is reporting to the chief of criminal investigation, Captain Eljuga, in the military police administration. All right, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see this document dated 31st of December 1995 from the military police crime investigation section of the 72nd. That was Major Milas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we see that this document is send to Major Eljuga in the military police administration crime investigation department. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so that we look at the subject of it, on the second page in the English, keeping the same page in the Croatian document, the subject of this letter was a report on the work of the military crime investigation police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion for the period of 25th of December 1994 to the 25th of December 1995. And this document is sent, as a report, to the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you aware that each year the 72nd would file a full report with the military police administration, detailing all their activities and work for the previous year?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. That's just as we were producing a yearly report for the battalion, so the battalion was doing the same for the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see from where Mr. Kay got the information that this document is going to the military police administration. It's referred to the Croatian Army Split Military District 72nd Military Police Battalion. It says military police crime investigation section --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It says it on page 1 in the English. Military police administration, military police crime investigation department, chief, Major Spomenko Eljuga, and we had established all that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question as to whom it was addressed. I believe I understood you to suggest that this document is going to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to figure out from where that -- I don't see that on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you assist Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it is quite clear from the document, Your Honour, what it says who it's to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you can you help me here, Mr. Simic, is it correct that this is addressed to the military police administration, military police crime investigation department, Major Eljuga?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may clarify, the heading in the top left corner says: "Croatian army, Split Military District. The 72nd Military Police Battalion was territorially within the AOR of Split, and of course it was sent by the 72nd MP Battalion, and it was sent to the Republic of Croatia Defence Ministry, military police administration, military police crime investigation department."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can go to page 6 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you have found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 6 of the English, which is page 5 of the Croatian document, I believe, under the heading "Introduction." It's page 4 in the Croatian document, yes, and I'm looking at the sentence at the foot of the page in English; "at the beginning of a new work year and looking back at 1995 ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in the middle of the page in Croatian, just below the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see where and pardon my language ability, pocetkom. I'm doing my best. With that sentence there: "At the beginning of a new work year and looking back at 1995, we're happy to say both horizontal and vertical cooperation was established between the KVP." And by "KVP," we mean what?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the section of the crime investigation military police of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, of the MP administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the KVP service, what does that refer to there?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the service of the various companies, the crime investigation military police section of the various companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that be the duty service?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is the MP crime investigation service, not the duty service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one, KVP department. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I was mistaken. The department of the crime MP is of -- is part of the administration, whereas the section of the KVP is -- belongs to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure if the witness said company or battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps can you tell us as to what those bodies refer to, Mr. Simic. There may be some difficulties. If you can explain that sentence to us, are you able to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The respective chain of commands. The service of the crime investigation MP was subordinated to the section which was subordinated to the department of the military police crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't need to go into that document any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D850, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D850 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 2643.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 3rd of November from the 72nd Military Police Battalion, military crime police department. That's Major Milas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And on that day, if we look to page 2 of the English, he sent this report to the military police administration, crime police department chief, Captain Eljuga. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see that it's a supplement to the report for the month of October 1995 and concerns deaths of HV soldiers. I have no need to refer to it in any more detail, the last page, page 4 in the English is signed by Major Milas, as you have already told us it was from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D851.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D851 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document is 65 ter 1616.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a document dated 5th of August, 1995 from the military police administration, military police crime investigation department. Can you see that, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was a yes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this was sent, as we can see, to the military police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that would be to the chief of the military police administration, is that right, General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see that it's an operative report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 5 of the English. In the Croatian version, that is page ... It's headed: Forward command post, page 3 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This concerns the forward command post of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. If we go to the second paragraph under there, can you see: "Therein in the course of the 4th of August, 1995, work meetings had been set up between all military police chiefs of the 72nd Military Police Battalion in Zadar, Sibenik, and Sinj, with the Major Boris Milas, chief of the 72nd Military Police Battalion ..." That means the crime investigation police battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You know who Major Milas is, because you've told us already, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I needed you to confirm in relation to this document. The rest of the document can speak for itself. And we can see on the last page that this is signed by Captain Eljuga of the police administration, as we know. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock and I noticed that from the 45 minutes you've used until now 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I had to field some objections which has lost me time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still speed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've only got three more documents to deal with, and I shall deal with them expeditiously, if I may. Thank you. May that lost document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time Ms. Mahindaratne I ask you whether you need -- you earlier talked about five questions whether it is still five.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Still five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still five. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry for being short as I'm trying to get through it. May that document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D852.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D852 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document is 65 ter 1935. It's a large document but I will deal with it very, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an report from the military police administration, military crime police department as we know that is a Captain Eljuga. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And this report, as we can see, written on the document by hand, is signed by Brigadier Biskic on the 6th of November, 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a report on the work of the military crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
