utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I need for these purposes. May this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D853, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D853 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have -- P495 is already in evidence, so I will skip that as that can be referred to later. May we see 65 ter 3533, which will be the last document, Your Honour. I'm grateful to the Court for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Simic, is dated the 30th of August, 1995, and it's from the military police administration, military police crime investigation department; and as we know, the chief of that is Captain Eljuga is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is sent to the 72nd Military Police Battalion crime investigation department, personally to the chief. It says Brigadier Milas but we know it is Major Milas, and it concerns a complaint in relation to the behaviour of HV troops and an UNCRO officer, Brigadier Al Rodan. And we can see at the end -- on the second page of the English that the 72nd is being required to expedite procedures for operational and criminal investigation processing by Captain Eljuga. It is underlined that last paragraph in the document in your language. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So this is an order from the military police administration chief, Captain Eljuga down to the 72nd. There is another page attach which is the complaint of the UNCRO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour I have no need to look at that as that is not the exercise I'm conducting and the evidence is obviously there. May this document be made an exhibit, Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D854, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D854 is admitted into evidence. Thank you Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne your five questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you stated in cross-examination that civilian police had the authority to use force to prevent the commission of crimes by members of the HV. Now, can you think any specific instance in which you know of where civilian police had used force to apprehend or bring perpetrator of the HV to your custody?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have a specific case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know of any factual situations where -- even if you can't think of details where that has happened?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was Major Boris Milas subordinated to Colonel Mihael Budimir within the 72nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... who was Major Milas immediate superior for his daily assignments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can get a clarification what daily assignments means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to daily assignments of the crime military police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Whom did he report to as his immediately superior on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Eljuga, or rather, my apologies he would report to Mihael Budimir on a daily basis or rather to the duty service about the activities carried out in his section.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred to seeing Major Juric and Ante Glavan visiting in the 4th Company, Sibenik, on one particular instance. And you said that they were there probably for agreement. Now what is the agreement that you were referring to that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the record I'm referring to transcript at page 55, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that Major Juric and Ante Glavan was there to meet your commander, Captain Mrkota, and you believed they were there for agreement. Can you specify as to what the agreement was, if you are aware of it?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that it did indeed involve and agreement. I said that I thought so, I believed so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you -- what was the agreement that you thought they were there to entail [sic] to?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: War agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you specify what do you mean by "war agreement"?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the work of the military police or about the work in general. I only make assumptions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question to you is, Mr. Simic, two question from the Bench, you referred to an instances where members of the 7th Guards Brigade had committed a crime, and you said that your crime police department had trouble collecting information because the brigade or some members of the brigade had withdrawn to barracks. Now what was the difficulty in obtaining collection -- sorry, collecting information regarding a crime or investigating a crime when a unit had withdrawn into barracks?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difficulty was the distance, and accessibility, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I notice when the witness has spoke about issue, that he mentioned the town from which originate the brigade, so maybe it would be wise to ask him about it. Because it didn't enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, he told, but it didn't enter the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, I don't intend to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, could you tell us where that -- where that brigade came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that it came from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Mr. President. May I just point out -- it's not with regard to re-examination but the Defence statement D840 that I believe is the number which was tendered during cross-examination of -- on behalf of Mr. Gotovina. One aspect Mr. Misetic probably could not address was paragraph 2 of the statement where there was agreement that the -- that he would address it in live testimony and now it is there and this is a matter in fact the Court had already dealt with through this witness at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're satisfy with the present position although Mr. Misetic did not raise the issue himself is that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would say that that paragraph should be excluded from the statement because it directly contradicts the testimony, and since Mr. Misetic did not address it in live testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour I was of the position up until the end here as well that you had addressed it with him directly and therefore there was no need to go into this again, so I ask that it stays in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it stay s in the statement and the parties now invite the Chamber to primarily consider the witness -- the testimony that the witness has given in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will consider whether it should be taken out or whether we can live with it. It is not of importance for this Chamber but if it would ever come to an appeal from -- raised by whatever party then of course it could create confusion. We'll consider it but at least, among these parties, it's clear what the status of that paragraph is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have one question for you, very short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said that you did some courses when you took up your new position. I see that you jointed the Ministry of Interior in January 1991 and that in November 1991 you were transferred to the 72nd Military Police Battalion. You explained that the courses were about drugs abuse and peacekeeping. In your statement, it reads that courses on investigation. Two questions. The first: When you worked for the MUP, or even prior to the MUP, did you receive any police training?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, drugs abuse, are you talking about investigation of drug offences; or are you talking about drugs abuse?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the crimes arising from drugs abuse and generally, yes, from the drugs -- drug addiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you worked as a military crime police officer. Having received - I leave apart your course on peacekeeping - you were functioning as it -- in your position as a military crime police officer with just an education, a course of drug abuse. Is that -- without any additional police training?

utterances.speaker: DAMIR SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any other training, and I carried out my line of duty, in accordance to -- with my abilities and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Have the questions in re-examination raised any need for further examination? If not, I would like to put one thing on the record. I earlier said it was one-to-one in tendering documents that were already in evidence. I was wrong. Ms. Mahindaratne, you're winning because 967 and 968 were not yet in evidence. I announced yesterday that they would be admitted into evidence once the redacted versions would have been uploaded. That was completed this morning, but I failed to establish that this completed the admission into evidence. Therefore, 967 and 968 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Simic, I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and to give your testimony, to have answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and that were put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then for the parties, we adjourn, and we resume on Monday, the 13th of October, 9.00 in this same Courtroom I, but not adjourn until after what I failed to do I think it was the day before yesterday, to thoroughly thank interpreters, transcribers all those who are assisting us, including security, for the extra time which I did not ask them whether it was granted but which I took. Apologies for that. We stand adjourned.
